title: The Link That Goes Quiet: Reads That Return Nothing, Writes That Do Not Finish

questions.question: A non blocking read returns zero. What has happened?
options: Nothing had arrived yet, which on a link polled faster than it talks is most calls
The device disconnected
The read failed
The stream reached its end
questions.explanation: Three returns, three meanings: positive is data, zero is silence, negative is an error. Collapsing zero into the error case gives a link that reports failure on an idle bus.

questions.question: write returns fewer bytes than you passed it. What goes out if you ignore that?
options: A truncated frame, which desynchronises the far end rather than simply being lost
Nothing, the write is retried automatically
The whole frame, since the count is advisory
A frame with a bad checksum, which the far end will reject cleanly
questions.explanation: A frame that is simply missing costs one message. One that is truncated costs the receiver its place in the stream, which is the failure the framing lesson was about.

questions.question: Why must a staleness clock be fed by valid messages rather than by bytes read?
options: A crashed device holding its line, or a motor inducing noise, produces bytes all day and no information
Reading the byte count is slower
Bytes arrive out of order
The byte count overflows
questions.explanation: A watchdog fed by bytes reports a dead link as healthy, and reports it most confidently when the noise is worst. Only a framed, checksummed, decoded message is evidence that somebody is there.

questions.question: One read returns two complete frames. What must the link do with the second?
options: Keep the unparsed bytes and continue from them on the next poll, since the read already took them out of the port
Read them again on the next poll
Deliver both messages from a single poll
Discard them, the sender will retransmit
questions.explanation: Bytes taken from the port are gone from it. Returning early without keeping the remainder loses every message after the first in a chunk, which on a busy link looks like a device that has halved its rate.

questions.question: Discards are high, frames received is zero. What does that pattern say?
options: The baud rate is wrong, or nothing is connected
A bad ground or a noisy cable
The device is alive and has stopped sending
The port never opened
questions.explanation: Frames arriving with checksums failing is the cable. Frames and checksums fine with nothing recent is a device that has stopped talking. Four numbers separate four faults that a single ok or failed cannot.

questions.question: Why does poll take the time as an argument instead of reading a clock?
options: A test can then make an hour pass instantly, so the staleness policy is checked rather than hoped about
Reading a clock is too slow inside a loop
The clock is not available on every platform
It keeps the function const
questions.explanation: The same seam as LoopMonitor in 07-03 and rate_limit in 01-02. A timeout you cannot test is a timeout you find out about in the field.
